Barnum will become vice chair, remaining with the bank until early 2028, JPMorgan said. Dimon added in a press release statement that Barnum had requested the transition after six years in the role. The announcement comes less than a week after Allison Beer, JPMorgan's head of credit card and connected commerce, informed colleagues that she was leaving to pursue another opportunity, according to an internal JPMorgan memo. Barnum's planned transition and Lake's retirement are part of a broader effort to prepare JPMorgan's next generation of leadership, according to a person familiar with the bank's succession planning. The person characterized Beer's departure as separate, saying the credit card executive was seeking a broader leadership role than her current responsibilities at the bank. title: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Mixed Ahead Of Much-Anticipated Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: SLS, BABA, JPM, OMER In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures traded mixed overnight late Monday as markets gear up for Nvidia Corp.’s (NVDA) third-quarter earnings on Tuesday and Anthropic's much-anticipated public listing on Wednesday. As of 10:37 p.m. EST, Dow futures declined 0.26%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.12% and Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.67%. On Monday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes closed lower amid a tech rout. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding more than 600 points to close 2.49% lower. The S&P 500 lost 1.92% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.41%. On Monday, markets took a beating as investors sold off Nvidia ahead of its Q3 results. The stock plunged more than 4% at close, dragging down other AI stocks and chipmakers. Nvidia’s results will need to prove that demand for its AI chips remains strong and that its growth outlook can sustain despite the recent leadership upheaval. New U.S. restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips and offshore computing power added to concerns over Nvidia’s leadership crisis and AI financing risks. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) fell more than 5% at close, while Micron Technology Inc. (MU) tumbled more than 7%. Broadcom Inc. (AVGO), Intel Corp. (INTC) and Marvell Technology Inc. (MRVL) also posted significant losses. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) also slumped about 5% each on Monday, while the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS) fell 2.51%. Charlie Bilello, Chief Market Strategist at Creative Planning, highlighted the sharp slide in NVDA stock following CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelity reports. In a post on X, he said, “Oct 6, 2026: Nvidia was up 28% YTD with a $5.8 trillion market cap, the world's largest. Today: After a 35% drawdown, Nvidia is now down 16% YTD with a market cap of $3.8 trillion. And Apple has reclaimed the world's top spot. $2 trillion erased in the last six weeks.” Meanwhile, Hideyuki Ishiguro, chief strategist at Nomura Asset Management, told Bloomberg that “Tighter restrictions could raise concerns about slowing sales growth and may weigh on earnings in the short term” for Asian chip-related firms. A potential catalyst for markets this week is Claude-maker Anthropic’s public listing, expected on Wednesday. The AI giant’s valuation could top $1.4 trillion, stoking a key test for Wall Street's AI appetite. Analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X, “Honestly, I think that the Anthropic IPO is likely going to go up first and then sideways, just like the SpaceX IPO. As a result, liquidity should flow back in due time.” Kenny Polcari, Chief Market Strategist at Slatestone Wealth, said in a post on X that the real test will be “how much future growth is already priced in—and what investors will pay for the AI boom,” even as its IPO is over 6x oversubscribed. On the geopolitical front, U.S. Vice President JD Vance vowed that the conflict with Iran would not become a prolonged “forever war” lasting two years. He also maintained that he remains aligned with Trump on Iran, acknowledged that the war contributed to Republican midterm losses through higher energy prices, and attributed those costs partly to decades of underinvestment in US energy infrastructure. Meanwhile, fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have been reported late Monday, raising security concerns in the pivotal shipping route and the prolonged tensions between the U.S. and Iran despite diplomatic efforts to end the war. Iran’s IRGC Navy said two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to cross the southern Strait of Hormuz via a route Tehran considers unauthorized. Oil prices have declined despite the rising tensions as U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that America would refrain from attacking Iran further. Brent crude futures were trading at $91.64 a barrel, down about 0.87%, while WTI crude futures traded 0.86% lower at $84.98 per barrel. Markets will also be watching for minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October meeting, when the central bank held the benchmark interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4.00% in a 10–2 vote, for further cues on the economy. Apart from Nvidia, Walt Disney Co. (DIS), Home Depot Inc. (HD) and Klarna Group (KLAR) are among the other companies slated to post their quarterly earnings. SELLAS Life Sciences Group Inc. (SLS): Shares of the clinical-stage biotechnology company were on the retail radar ahead of its highly anticipated Phase 3 REGAL trial results for galinpepimut-S (GPS) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) this month after hitting the 80th event threshold in late October. JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM): The American bank garnered attention amid a banking outage due to a software bug. Several other U.S. banks, including Wells Fargo (WFC) and Bank of America (BAC) were also experiencing issues. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (BABA): The Chinese technology and e-commerce giant is caught in the crossfire as investors debate whether Nvidia’s chip restrictions could impact its AI ambitions. Omeros Corp. (OMER): The biopharmaceutical company’s stock fell nearly 7% overnight after it reported Q3 results that reported a headline GAAP net loss large enough to rattle investors. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) edged higher in the overnight session, while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) was down at the time of writing. U.S. Treasury yields climbed — the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading at 5.129%, while the 30-year yield was at 5.476%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was down 0.09% amid ‘neutral’ sentiment. Asian markets opened lower on Tuesday, with South Korea's KOSPI, Japan’s Nikkei 225, China’s SSE Composite and Australian stocks all trading lower at the time of writing. Chip stocks eased in post-market hours on Monday after a sharp drop in the regular session triggered by new U.S. chip curbs targeting AI capacity available to Chinese companies. SK Hynix (SKHY) led the overnight gains, rising 3.6%. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Micron (MU) rose 2% and 2.8% respectively and Broadcom (AVGO) gained 2.3% in what appears to be a relief rally. AMD, MU and AVGO fell between 4% and 7.6% in Monday’s session as investors took the new U.S. technology export curbs as a potential headwind for chip sales. Intel (INTC), which fell 7%, continued to be in the red in overnight trading as Nvidia disclosed it trimmed its stake in the government-backed chipmaker. The Donald Trump administration on Monday moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, following increased scrutiny over its handling of curbs on semiconductor exports after an alleged spy scandal involving Nvidia Corp (NVDA). An interim rule issued by the Commerce Department now requires data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a license from Washington before exporting advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other U.S. manufacturers to customers in those countries. The measure is an attempt to restrict China and other U.S. adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses high-end American processors. The government’s directive came days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following his admission to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the U.S. authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. Megaspeed was already under a U.S. investigation for possible export control violations. Nvidia will report third-quarter results on Tuesday and will likely face tough questions about Huang and the chipmaker's dealings with Megaspeed. SemiAnalysis founder Dylan Patel said more than 1.5 gigawatts of chips are in China in violation of U.S. law, and warned that efforts to trace how they got there could reshape the AI industry. “That whole web” is now set to unwind, he said in a SemiAnalysis video interview. Patel also questioned whether open-source AI can thrive if Nvidia can no longer support it, calling the ecosystem “a lot weaker with NVIDIA down and out.” He said that shift could leave Anthropic closer to a monopoly or duopoly, a prospect he said “bodes really well” for its IPO this week, although Anthropic is “more diverse in what chips they use than any other company in the world.” Meanwhile, Nvidia disclosed its latest holdings. It cut its stake in Intel by 25% in the third quarter, selling about 53.69 million shares, and now holds 161.08 million shares. The disclosure weighed on Intel’s shares in post market hours. Nvidia also trimmed positions in Nokia and Synopsys during the quarter, while increasing its SpaceX stake. To be sure, investors such as Soros Fund Management, Barclays and Assenagon Asset Management increased their Intel stakes in Q3. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ for BABA, ‘bullish’ for AMD and AVGO, ‘neutral’ for MU, and ‘bearish’ for INTC. “$INTC Unfortunately, we have some gullible investors who are selling after every panic-inducing post/article. It should be the other way around, especially at current prices,” said a trader. “$MU trend reversal. Now in uptrend in overnight trading. Higher tomorrow for sure,” wrote another. Over the next three months, Nvidia cut its Intel share count by 25% and added 7.71 million SpaceX shares. SpaceX was the only one of the eight stocks in Nvidia’s filing in which it reported owning more shares. SpaceX took the top spot even as the value of Nvidia’s stake fell from $20.98 billion to $19.68 billion. Its Intel holding fell further, to $19.37 billion. By Sept. 30, Nvidia owned 130.47 million SpaceX shares, and its former No. 2 holding was ahead by $316 million. Appaloosa went from 225,000 SpaceX shares in June to 3.88 million in September. The 1,626% jump in share count turned a $38.4 million position into one valued at $556.5 million. SpaceX accounted for 7% of the fund’s disclosed portfolio, behind only Micron Technology, Amazon and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. Druckenmiller’s Duquesne started smaller. Its June filing listed no SpaceX shares. By September, it held 202,125 shares, worth about $30.5 million at the quarter-end closing price. Meanwhile, Australian mining billionaire Gina Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting already owned more SpaceX shares than Appaloosa and Duquesne combined. Its September filing showed 8,000,005 shares, up from exactly 8 million in June. As SpaceX’s stock price fell, the stake lost about $160 million in value, ending the quarter at $1.21 billion. It still accounted for a fifth of Hancock’s disclosed portfolio. Hancock made its bigger moves in defense. It opened an 80,000-share position in General Dynamics worth about $26.5 million and added to its holdings in RTX, Northrop Grumman, L3Harris Technologies and Lockheed Martin. On Monday, two of Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management funds bought a combined 378,515 SpaceX shares, while selling 543,092 Nvidia shares. The ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought 341,030 SpaceX shares, and the ARK Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW) added 37,485. ARK bought two days after SpaceX’s launch tower in Texas caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit for the first time. The spacecraft had deployed 26 Starlink satellites before returning to the launch site. SpaceX missed the planned booster catch, leaving a double catch as the next milestone in its effort to reuse the entire rocket. “Grateful to @elonmusk and his incredible SpaceX Team for changing the course of history!” Wood said on X. Last week, SpaceX outlined plans for over $74 billion in Texas and Arizona AI facilities, after last month’s roughly $40 billion lease commitment through an Apollo-managed entity for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips and related equipment. Ken Griffin’s Citadel Advisors held 283,822 SpaceX shares at the end of September, down 95% from 5.13 million in June. Its options positions grew, with calls covering 20.57 million shares and puts covering 12.31 million, both more than double their June levels. Separately, SpaceX director Antonio J. Gracias reported that his ownership fell from 6.5% to 5.5% of Class A shares. Valor-affiliated entities held most of those shares. Bitcoin (BTC) is struggling to find its footing after the weekend selloff, and the options market is showing signals on the downside. With Nvidia (NVDA) set to report earnings after market close on Tuesday, rising Treasury yields and weakening spot Bitcoin ETF flows are adding to concerns for the cryptocurrency’s performance. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday and plummeted to around $62,000 over the weekend, before recovering to $64,000 late Monday. Now analysts warn that a weak report from Nvidia could push it below $60,000. Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, said the $60,000 to $62,600 range is the key test in the next few weeks. Nvidia's disappointing report could spark another wave of selling across risk assets, he said. "AI and crypto draw on the same pool of risk capital, so when Nvidia sells off, the money goes to cash, not into bitcoin," Søndergaard told Coindesk. Søndergaard is looking for a break above the 200-day moving average near $73,000 as the first sign that the selling is done. Bitcoin’s price was trading at $64,490, down over 1% in the last 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC dropped to the ‘bearish’ zone from the ‘neutral’ zone over the past day. Chatter around it rose over 38% over the past week, according to platform data. The Over-the-Counter (OTC) desk of crypto market maker Wintermute, which facilitates large trades away from public exchanges, said that Bitcoin is still in a bear market. Coindesk reported that the desk sees little sign of new inflows in to fuel a recovery. The OTC desk said rising rates have changed how investors treat Bitcoin. "This is a rates tape in which bitcoin is the non-yielding funding leg, the ETF bid is gone and the technicals have broken, so we stay defensive and the path of least resistance still feels lower,” the desk added. Wintermute predicts Bitcoin to face pressure around the $50,000 range. The next levels to watch were identified as $62,000 and then $60,000. The desk said much of the pressure is coming from the bond market. Traders see about a 92% chance the Federal Reserve will again raise rates in December. The 10-year Treasury yield is up to 5.15%. The two calls among the top eight were the $65,000 and $75,000 strikes expiring Dec. 25. The $75,000 call jumped 46.67%, a sign some traders are betting on a bounce. The companies also agreed to explore using Nokia’s optical technology and switches to move data through Nvidia’s AI infrastructure. The group plans to bid for an EU contract to build and operate a network of computing sites that European businesses, researchers and public agencies could use to run AI workloads. Nokia will supply the networking equipment to move data securely between the sites. The partners have selected Oulu in Finland, Iru in Estonia and Valmiera in Latvia, and are still choosing a location in Sweden. Additionally, Nokia signed a multiyear agreement licensing its video tech for use in ASUS devices. The deal resolves all related patent litigation between the companies. Nokia has contributed to several generations of video compression standards, which help devices store and stream video using less data. The companies kept the financial terms confidential. Lilly’s potential maximum payout was close to Sellas’ entire $1.52 billion market value at Monday’s close, and its lead leukemia drug is already awaiting Phase 3 results. Calytrix is developing an antibody that targets a mutation behind two rare blood cancers, essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis. Lilly will make an undisclosed upfront payment. title: Why Are US Banks Reporting Outages? JPMorgan Rules Out Cyberattack, Blames Software Bug - TradingView
content: Users at multiple American banks, including JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), reported outages of banking services late Monday, with some retail users speculating about a cybersecurity attack. However, JPMorgan denied evidence of cybersecurity attacks and attributed the outage to a software bug. According to DownDetector, apart from JPMorgan, service disruptions were also reported at Bank of America Corp. (BAC), Wells Fargo & Co. (WFC), Capital One Financial Corp. (COF), and U.S. Bancorp. (USB). As per the website, 33% of the issues reported at JPMorgan were related to the website, while 32% reported issues with fund transfers and 20% reported login troubles. Meanwhile, at Wells Fargo, users reported challenges with account balances or transactions, login and digital payment service Zelle. At Bank of America, US Bank and Capital One, troubles ranged from ATM and online banking to app-related issues. JPMorgan said in a post on X, “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.” The bank added that as a party to transactions involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted as well, but clarified that this was not a systemic issue. “Customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today,” it said. Banking Outage Follows Disruptions At Microsoft, FAA Last Week The issues at JPMorgan and other banks come shortly after Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) suffered a widespread outage across Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services on Thursday, which continued into Friday last week. Meanwhile, a technical network overload caused by a router update and data flood forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026, halting all flight departures across U.S. airports for nearly five hours. Retail users on Stocktwits acknowledged the “weird” coincidence of multiple outages within a short period of time across industries. One user said, “$QQQ $SPY First $MSFT is down, Then FAA gets affected. Now the "bugs" are hitting $JPM. What's next, ATMs down (unable to process withdrawls)?” Another user said, “$JPM AI has become the boogey man ...any glitch etc is bc of ai. Its mass hysteria. But thats what kept us from forming a bubble in the stock market.” A third user said, “$JPM just sayin seems weird this last week.” JPM stock is down about 0.15% overnight, while WFC has lost about 0.17%, and COF and USB are trading marginally higher in the same time. title: JP Morgan Chase Wins North American Corporate Chess League Season 14 - Chess.com
content: JP Morgan Chase won the 14th season of the North American Corporate Chess League in an exciting final match against PWC, taking the title 3-2. It was the banking company's first championship. The company fielded a strong team led by IM Edward Song, FMs Alex Bian and Maggie Feng, NM Asuka Nakamura (brother of GM Hikaru Nakamura), and Calvin Yang. You can see coverage of the knockout matches, hosted by GM Kayden Troff, below. A successful regular season earned JP Morgan Chase the top seed entering the knockout phase. In the quarterfinals they faced the tech company NVIDIA, led by IM Bogdan-Gabriel Vioreanu. Song faced technical issues to start the playoffs and forfeited his game against Vioreanu. That was the only victory for NVIDIA, while Yang and Nakamura scored for JP Morgan Chase to take a tight match, 3-2. In the semifinals, JP Morgan Chase faced Susquehanna, who had defeated the defending champions, Jane Street, in the previous round. Nakamura led the way again with a critical victory, while Bian defeated Brian Luo in a sharp game. Nicolas Brinkman struck back for Susquehanna by defeating Yang, but it wasn't enough. JP Morgan Chase advanced 3-2, earning a spot in the finals. PWC was led by GM Andrey Baryshpolets, and they defeated Meta to earn a finals matchup against JP Morgan Chase. Baryshpolets defeated Song in a complicated game, and PWC's Mark Morrison moved to 3/3 on the day by defeating Yang. JP Morgan Chase struck on the other boards. Nakamura won his third game of the day, defeating NM David Siamon. Bian defeated Michael Giampa and Feng defeated Alexander Fogel in a tricky endgame. Feng's victory clinched the title for JP Morgan Chase, winning the match 3-2 and bringing the company its first title in the 14-year history of the league. The North American Corporate Chess League brings together companies headquartered in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico for seven weeks of team chess competition on Chess.com. title: Inflation, a fragmented world and the next phase of AI: Where investors may find risk and opportunity in 2027 - Chase Bank
content: It appears your web browser is not using JavaScript. Without it, some pages won't work properly. Please adjust the settings in your browser to make sure JavaScript is turned on. As 2026 draws to a close, investors have had to navigate an unusual mix of market gains and mounting pressures. The S&P 500 has reached new record highs, even as conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy markets, inflation remained above central bank targets and bond yields climbed. Meanwhile, enthusiasm for AI has continued to drive investment – along with tougher questions about what returns that spending will ultimately generate. Inflation, global fragmentation and AI are not new themes, having previously anchored our 2026 Mid-Year Outlook. But heading into 2027, the growing need to finance AI and security is changing what it costs to invest in them – and what investors can earn in return. Technology companies need capital to build AI infrastructure, while governments need it to strengthen defense, energy security and supply chains. At the same time, inflation and higher interest rates have made financing more expensive but have also given investors more choices about where to put their money. What they choose to fund – and at what price – will help shape the next phase of progress. In its newly released 2027 Outlook, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management examines how these forces may shape markets and investment decisions in the year ahead. “The three forces of AI, fragmentation, and inflation have been validated throughout 2026 through the dramatic AI capex and earnings super cycle, the energy supply shock of the U.S. / Iran conflict, and through central banks that have been forced to tighten policy to promote inflation-fighting credibility,” J.P. Morgan Wealth Management’s Chief Investment Strategist Phil Camporeale said. “Simply put, these three forces appear to be deepening rather than fading. Through all of this, we remain constructive on diversified multi-asset portfolios heading into 2027, but that constructive view depends on a few key assumptions.” The opportunities are significant, but they are not all alike. Here’s what investors should watch for in 2027. Inflation may moderate in 2027, but that does not mean a return to the low interest rate environment that investors grew accustomed to before the pandemic. Energy prices have added to inflation pressures, and central banks are weighing how far they might need to raise rates. Slower wage growth and a stable labor market suggest policymakers may be able to contain inflation without bringing the economic expansion to an end. For investors, higher rates cut both ways. They make it more expensive for companies and governments to borrow, but they also change what investors can earn when they lend. The challenge is to take advantage of that shift while remaining prepared for another potential inflation shock. "We assume that central bankers are hiking rates as part of a mid-cycle adjustment to maintain credibility," said Camporeale. "We don’t anticipate the kind of aggressive hiking that often accompanies the end of a business cycle." Central banks may not need to raise rates aggressively. Slower wage growth and a stable labor market support the view that inflation could moderate without a sharp rate-hiking campaign. Faster wage growth could change that calculation, however. A sustained energy shock poses a different problem: It could push prices higher while weakening demand, leaving central banks with a harder choice between containing inflation and supporting growth. Inflation can still erode purchasing power. Even if the overall inflation rate falls, the prices that matter most to an investor may rise faster than the headline measure. That makes it worth thinking about future spending needs, not just whether inflation is moving closer to a central bank’s target. Higher yields give investors more choices. High-quality bonds now offer more income than they did during the low-rate era, making them a more compelling option for investors seeking returns. Their prices can still fall if yields rise further, though, so a higher starting yield doesn’t remove short-term risk. Stocks and bonds may not always offset each other. When an inflation shock puts pressure on both asset classes, a traditional stock and bond portfolio may offer less protection than investors expect. Real assets and other diversifying strategies may be worth considering alongside that foundation, depending on an investor’s goals and risk tolerance. Work 1:1 with our advisors to help build a personalized financial strategy that’s built around you. Conflict can disrupt markets quickly. But the longer-term investment story is how countries respond, which often involves spending more on defense, energy security and supply chains they can depend on. Those efforts require substantial financing and may create opportunities for businesses that help make economies more resilient. Those opportunities are not confined to traditional defense companies – or to the United States. They span industries and regions, from chipmaking and manufacturing to power infrastructure and critical materials. But a more fragmented world also makes it more important to distinguish between countries that can finance their ambitions and companies that may benefit from the spending. "While geopolitical fragmentation can act as a drag on global growth, we also think it could lead to a meaningful increase in capital expenditure in both the public and private sectors, which can drive nominal growth," said Camporeale. "Investors must be selective about where countries sit on the spectrum of natural resources, vulnerabilities to supply bottlenecks, and their ability to defend themselves." Security spending could benefit companies across the globe. European businesses are capturing orders tied to rearmament and advanced technology. South Korea, Taiwan and Japan supply semiconductors and other equipment that countries need to expand their AI capabilities, while Mexico could benefit as companies move production closer to the United States. The opportunities differ by region, but all reflect a greater willingness to spend on security and reliable supply chains. A country’s vulnerabilities can change the investment case. Its ability to defend itself, develop AI infrastructure, obtain essential supplies and adapt to climate risks all matter. Europe shows why those distinctions are important: Companies could gain from spending on resilience, while the governments financing that spending may face pressure from higher debt and borrowing costs. Energy and critical materials remain potential bottlenecks. Building data centers, expanding power grids and strengthening domestic industries all require reliable energy and materials such as copper. Supply can take years to catch up with demand, making these resources important both to the AI buildout and to national resilience. Alongside their role in these industries, commodities may help diversify portfolios during periods when inflation weighs on both stocks and bonds. Gold offers a different way to navigate fragmentation. Some countries are seeking to hold more of their reserves outside the dollar-based system, and central banks are holding more gold as a share of their overall reserves. That shift could support demand for gold for reasons distinct from the need for energy and metals to build infrastructure. The first phase of the AI boom rewarded companies supplying the chips, equipment and power needed to execute it. Heading into 2027, the question is shifting from how much infrastructure can be built to whether enough people and businesses will use AI – and pay for it – to justify the investment. That doesn’t mean the AI opportunity is ending. AI could still boost productivity and corporate profits, but the scale of the buildout makes it more important to distinguish between companies that can turn demand into durable revenue and those counting on another surge in spending. "We assume that AI adoption may spur continued productivity gains as business use cases expand. AI needs to earn its keep by delivering real value to an economy rather than just answer questions," said Camporeale. "According to the firm’s 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, we believe the U.S. economy could see a 50% boost in productivity in the next 10-15 years. We believe hyperscalers may be well positioned to take advantage of this next phase of the AI trade from buildout to adoption." AI needs to move beyond early adopters. Businesses are experimenting with AI, but widespread use is still in its early stages. For the buildout to pay off, more companies will need to use AI in everyday work, and consumers will need to find uses they value. Adoption could slow if the technology falls short of expectations – or if job disruption and public opposition make its wider use harder to sustain. The buildout has a high revenue hurdle. J.P. Morgan Wealth Management estimates that, in the early 2030s, customers would need to spend roughly $2.9 trillion a year on AI to cover the costs of global data center capacity projected for the end of 2029. An illustrative estimate puts potential annual spending by businesses, consumers and governments at about $3.6 trillion. Neither figure is assured: Both depend on how much capacity is built, how widely AI is adopted and what customers ultimately pay. How companies finance AI matters. Large cloud providers generally have stronger balance sheets and more established businesses to help fund their investments. Some smaller companies rely much more heavily on borrowing to build capacity before they have the revenue to support it. If investors become less willing to finance those plans, access to capital could determine which projects move forward and which companies struggle. The next AI winners may look different from the first. Chipmakers and other infrastructure suppliers benefited as spending on the buildout repeatedly exceeded expectations. Further surprises may be harder to deliver as financing, power availability and resistance to new data centers constrain construction. But a slower build could also make scarce computing capacity more valuable. Major cloud providers may be well positioned because they both supply that capacity and sell services built on it; over time, companies that turn AI into products customers pay for could capture more value. The price of progress is becoming clearer. Building AI infrastructure and making economies more secure both require enormous amounts of capital, while inflation and higher interest rates have made that capital more expensive. For investors, the opportunity is not simply to fund those ambitions, but to be selective about which risks might be worth taking. That suggests considering a portfolio designed to pursue long-term growth without depending on every part of the AI buildout paying off or inflation fading smoothly. Not working with us yet? title: Lilly secures another myelofibrosis option via $1.5B deal for JPM-founded Calytrix - Fierce Biotech
content: Eli Lilly has added another myelofibrosis (MF) play to its pipeline courtesy of a $1.5 billion deal for Massachusetts biotech Calytrix Bio. The prize for Lilly is a biparatopic antibody for mutant calreticulin (mCALR)-driven essential thrombocythemia (ET) and MF, which are both rare blood cancers. Calytrix has touted the preclinical antibody as a way to deliver “disease-modifying pan-mutant activity, with a safety and convenience profile that supports early intervention and long-term treatment.” While current treatments for ET and MF primarily manage symptoms and complications, Calytrix spied an opportunity for a precision therapy targeting the CALR mutation that drives the disease. Under the deal, Calytrix’s shareholders could receive up to $1.5 billion cash spread across upfront and milestone payments—although the companies didn’t offer a detailed breakdown of the financials. Lilly already has an MF asset in its pipeline courtesy of the phase 1-stage type II JAK2 inhibitor AJ1-11095 which was the focus of the Big Pharma’s $2.3 billion deal for Ajax Therapeutics in April. That bet appeared to pay off two months later when 70% of patients achieved a best response of at least a 35% reduction in spleen volume in early results from a phase 1 study. In a note to investors this morning, Citi analysts suggested that Calytrix’s preclinical asset was a good strategic fit alongside AJ1-11095, as the newly acquired candidate targets the disease-driving clone rather than downstream JAK signaling. “The biparatopic design targets both major mCALR mutation types, which together are found in roughly one-quarter of ET and primary MF patients,” the analysts noted. “While scientifically attractive, the program remains preclinical, and the safety bar will be particularly high in indolent ET.” “An mCALR-specific antibody could be evaluated alone or potentially alongside a JAK2 inhibitor, although combination strategy, dosing and the ability to reverse established marrow fibrosis remain unproven,” the analysts concluded. Calytrix was built last year by J.P. Morgan’s life sciences venture capital arm with a mission to develop disease-modifying therapies for patients living with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). “Calytrix was founded on the belief that patients with MPNs deserve therapies that do more than manage symptoms,” the biotech’s CEO Brad Prosek said in a Nov. 16 release. “From the beginning, our goal has been to alter the disease course in mCALR-driven ET and MF,” Prosek added. “We look forward to Lilly advancing the program through the clinic and exploring its potential to benefit patients across the disease spectrum.” The Calytrix acquisition caps off a hectic year of buyouts for Lilly. Fueled by sales of its GLP-1 drugs, the company has inked a series of takeovers and licensing pacts, penning multibillion-dollar deals with biotechs including AtaiBeckley, Centessa Pharmaceuticals and Kelonia Therapeutics.

title: JP Morgan forecasts 2% monthly inflation in Argentina in 2027 - Buenos Aires Herald
content: According to a report by J.P. Morgan, Argentina will head into the 2027 presidential election with monthly inflation stabilized at around 2%. However, the United States financial institution warned that a possible resurgence of foreign exchange market tensions in the coming months could force it to revise its forecast upward. “The risks are tilted to the upside if exchange-rate-related pressures prove stronger than expected, amid growing domestic and global uncertainty,” economists Lucila Barbeito and Diego Pereira said in a report sent to the bank’s clients. The forecast is in line with those of major local consulting firms, which expect little change in the pace of inflation and, in that context, economic activity. It is worth noting that the outlook is more encouraging than the one left by Alberto Fernández’s government, although it contrasts with the expectations held by Javier Milei and his economic team for the country’s economic trajectory. The prospect of inflation “starting with a zero” remains a long way off, judging by bond prices. J.P. Morgan highlighted that cumulative inflation through October reached 26.3%, compared with 24.8% over the same period in 2025. For the final two months of 2026, the bank forecast an average monthly inflation rate of 1.9%, consistent with a year-on-year rate of 31% in December. This would leave annual inflation just half a percentage point below the 31.5% recorded in 2025. For the first quarter of 2027, the bank projected average monthly inflation of 1.8%, driven by the impact of the El Niño weather phenomenon on food prices and concentrated increases in public utility rates. “In the second half of 2027, we expect monthly inflation to average 1.9%, reflecting pressure on prices of tradable goods in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) amid election-driven volatility,” the economists said. October inflation stood at 2.2%, above the 1.8% forecast by the Central Bank’s Market Expectations Survey. Increases in gas rates and vegetable prices gained momentum during the month. Core inflation, which excludes regulated and seasonal prices, eased to 1.5%, its lowest level in almost 18 months. “Inflation is expected to end 2026 at around 31%, a level very similar to last year’s 31.5%. 2027 would begin with inflation holding steady at 1.9% per month, equivalent to an annualized rate of 25%, with upside risks amid the electoral process,” Fundación Capital, led by Martín Redrado, said in a report published last week. “Looking ahead, convergence toward lower levels will take time and should ideally be supported only by solid and sustainable fundamentals, such as fiscal balance and prudent monetary policy, avoiding artificial anchors that can prove distortionary and build up risks over time,” the consulting firm said. In the short term, consulting firm Econviews estimated that November inflation would be around 1.8%. Its survey showed a 1.7% increase in food and beverage prices over the past four weeks, with vegetable prices falling during the first half of the month. Meanwhile, increases in public transportation, electricity and water rates were announced, while private health plans and internet services also became more expensive. “Nevertheless, inflationary inertia remains strong, and it is difficult to expect a significant decline in inflation,” the consultancy led by Miguel Kiguel said. Meanwhile, Invecq’s survey recorded a 2.2% increase in its four-week moving average, a pace similar to October’s. The consultancy estimated that inflation would reach 31.2% in 2026 if the 1.9% monthly average recorded between August and October were repeated over the final two months of the year. It also focused on meat prices, which rose just 0.1% in October, compared with increases of 6.2% in November and 7.9% in December 2025. For Invecq, “the fundamental challenge remains breaking inflationary inertia.” The consultancy noted that many services continue to adjust their prices in line with past inflation. In October, service prices rose 2.7%, while goods prices increased 1.9%. During the first 10 months of the year, the respective increases reached 33.8% and 22.6%. It is worth noting that in March, Milei had said he expected consumer inflation to “start with a zero” in August, meaning a monthly rate below 1%. That month, the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INDEC, in Spanish) recorded inflation at 1.7%. In September, presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier raised the possibility of inflation reaching “zero point something” by October 2027. In a scenario where monthly inflation stabilizes at around 2%, collective bargaining negotiations and nominal incomes would need to exceed that threshold to restore purchasing power. According to a report by consulting firm LCG, registered private-sector wages rose 1.9% in September, matching the increase in the Consumer Price Index. As a result, real wages stood 0.8% below their December 2025 level and 2.3% below November 2023. The consultancy said occasional improvements were possible but warned that “without a stronger recovery in economic activity, it will be difficult to sustain an improvement in real wages.” Stagnant incomes are also limiting the recovery in consumption. “The main difficulty at this point is that economic activity and growth in real incomes are weak, creating uncertainty about the continuity of policies,” Barclays said in a report to its clients. The British bank said this uncertainty had become investors’ main concern and helped explain the impact of recent international shocks on Argentina’s country risk. Barclays noted that the Central Bank had purchased around US$16 billion since January, exceeding market expectations. It also warned that the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections could reduce the government’s room to repeat the foreign exchange assistance it received in 2025. If uncertainty over the economic program fuels demand for dollars ahead of the elections, the government will find it harder to maintain exchange-rate stability. A sharp depreciation that feeds through to prices could push inflation above J.P. Morgan’s baseline forecast.
